Banking-Phone Scam

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Unbeknown to you, a sim swop is done on your phone. The criminal then hacks into your banking details, transfers all your money to another account and leave you with nothing.

Summary:
You might only think there is something wrong with your phone signal - your service provider is busy with maintenance in the area or it's just one more "bad signal day". Think again and be aware - because during this time that your phone is not working, an illegal and unauthorised sim swop could be taking place - directing all your messages to the criminal's phone, including your bank's One Time Pins (OTP's), with which you authorise transactions on your bank accounts.

Further information:
How the criminal gains access to the victim's online banking details is still unclear. Most of our case studies say they know what phishing scams are and they haven't entered their details into any of these websites. All the case studies have been long-standing Nedbank clients.

The scam works as follows:

- without the victims knowledge or authorisation, a sim swop is done on his/her Vodacom phone
- all mesages, including all One Time Pins to authorise online banking transactions, are then send to the criminal's phone who has done the sim swop
- the criminal uses the victim's banking details to log into their online banking
- the criminal then withdraws from the victim's credit, bond, overdraft etc to the maximum limit and transfers all this money into the victim's current account, before paying it into another Nedbank account
- all of the transactions are authorised via OTP's which are sent to the criminal's cellphone instead of the victims, thanks to the sim swop
- the money is withdrawn from the criminal's account (sometimes in cash) and becomes, according to Nedbank, untraceable

It seems to be a quite sophisticated scam

Press Release:


Phishing season explodes
Bank-related internet fraud is the fastest-growing crime in the world. Criminals trick customers into disclosing private information that they use to empty their unsuspecting victims’ bank accounts. But just how sophisticated can tech-savvy criminals get? Carte Blanche investigates the complexities of the latest “phishing trip”.


Script:


NEDBANK-VODACOM SCAM

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

Money stashed in a piggy bank… in a tin… under the mattress…in a book… in a tea pot – just to keep it safe! Those days are long gone …

We keep our money in the bank and trust that it will be safe and secure.
But is it?

FRANZ KRUGER: I pay them chunks of money in all sorts of different forms to look after my money. They didn’t, that’s the bottom line.

NOEL GARDNER: You would think that if anything undesirable happened in your account, at least somebody is going to be checking.

DR. FANUS LUES: It’s their responsibility to take good care of your money.

DEVI: Otherwise, why put your money in the bank?

DR. FANUS LUES: You can put it underneath your bed if you want to.

A dentist; a journalism lecturer and a businessman.

All three are victims of a highly evolved phishing or internet banking scam.
While there is no investigative link between their cases, similarities are evident in how the fraud against them was perpetrated.

DEVI: Is it easy to fall prey?

DANNY MYBURGH: It’s very easy to fall prey. We see doctors, we see pensioners, students tech savvy people. No-one is immune against this.

DEVI LINK: It’s faceless and borderless. Phishing scams are a global phenomenon and run by highly sophisticated syndicates.

DANNY MYBURGH: All they need to do is put up a website in the Ukraine its difficult for us to gain access to it, they send out masses of mails from an email cafe in Nigeria and then a person in Cape Town sits and forwards that information onto somebody sitting in America.

KALYANI PILLAY/SABRIC: We had an increase of the amount of phishing scams detected between 2013/2014 of 31%.

DEVI: Are phishing scams unique to one bank?

KALYANI PILLAY/SABRIC: It actually is not about the bank. It is about trying to get information of individuals who have bank accounts. They just go for it, so they don’t care about a bank’s brand.

DANNY MYBURGH/CYBER EXPERT: We do see that they focus on a specific bank or on a specific cellphone company and as soon as those banks or cellphone companies increase their security they move onto the next target.

In 2010, we brought you a story about a syndicate that had its sights on Standard Bank.

DEVI LINK: Carte Blanche recently received several complaints from phishing victims – all banking with Nedbank, all with Vodacom contracts.


Our three case studies’ stories include a sim swop they never asked for;
mystery beneficiaries added to their banking profile;
and large sums of money transferred from their accounts without their authorisation.

So, how does the scam work?

It all starts with a phishing email enticing you to reveal personal information, such as your banking details and cellphone number.

DEVI LINK: There are two ways in which you can be compromised via an email. You click on a link and you are taken to a fake website or you click on a link and spyware is immediately installed on your computer.

Once fraudsters have your personal details, they’ll need access to your cellphone number to authorise banking transactions.
Pretending to be you, they process a sim swop at your service provider.
They then log onto your banking profile, create a new beneficiary and clear out your accounts.

Dr Lues lost R735 000, Professor Kruger R85 000 and Noel Gardner R150 000.

DEVI LINK: You may think you haven’t fallen prey to one of these phishing emails, but it’s not so obvious.

DANNY MYBURGH: If you click on a specific link it will take you through to a bank site that is representative of the real bank site, so for example it could be one of the banks, it could be SARS.

ADV. CLIVE PILLAY: The sites are very cleverly developed and they look almost identical to a legitimate site.

At first glance, both these Nedbank sites look authentic. On closer inspection one sees differences: like the authentic site’s URL and padlock.

ADV. CLIVE PILLAY: That padlock is incapable of being replicated.

The fake website also asks for your phone number, something a bank would NEVER do.

ANTON DE WET: People need to understand it’s not the bank’s systems that have been compromised. Nedbank is secure, the issue here in each other incidences will be where the persons private information has been compromised.

KALYANI PILLAY/SABRIC: The perpetrators will use social engineering techniques to get you to give them information and you don’t even sometimes know that you are doing it.

DEVI: Did you go click on any weird looking URL’s?

NOEL: No.

DEVI: Are you sure?

NOEL: Yes.

DEVI: Hundred percent?

NOEL: Yes.

DANNY: There is so many different variants - I can send out an email to say: “Please look at the attached photograph, I picked up this camera, see if you recognise the couple.” As soon as you click on the attachment the virus is installed.

DEVI: So when you do ask somebody did you click on something funny the answer is no because that’s not funny that was just a mistake?

DANNY: It’s as simple as that.

The sim swop also seems to be quite simple.

DANNY: They will pretend to be you, they will say that your cellphone was stolen and apply for a new simcard, and the next moment you are not receiving any transactions on your cellphone, they are receiving it, and they are transferring your money.

Although not the case with all cellphone providers - at Vodacom you don’t have to do the sim swop in person, but can do it over the phone.

RICHARD: When you call the call centre, what then happens is, we send an sms to you to say a sim swop is being performed on this sim, if you did not request this, please get in touch with us. There is then a two-hour delay, and if there is no contact in those two hours, then the sim swop goes ahead.

Dr. Lues’s online banking profile is linked to his PA’s phone. She did receive such an SMS.

DR. LUES: Before she could answer, she got another phone call to say that it was sent to the wrong number, she must completely ignore it.

Vodacom confirmed that a call centre employee was arrested in connection with Dr Lues’ case, for working with a cybercrime syndicate.
Franz’s sim swop happened when he switched from one network to another and Noel’s while his phone was switched off.

NOEL: Lots of phone calls, each time I picked it up, nothing. My wife said to switch it off.

RICHARD: They will call you, you answer the phone, they hang up. Call you, you answer, they hang up, call you hang up… What they are trying to get you to do, is switch the phone off in frustration and once you’ve done that, they do the sim swop, two hours later, they’ve got access to your bank account.

DEVI LINK: So whose to blame: your cellphone service provider, your bank or you?

Prof Kruger refuses to shoulder all the blame.

FRANZ: There are three elements here: the one is my online banking profile, right? Okay, so the bank claims I am at fault there. The other element is he phone and there is clearly no way that I have any responsibility there. The third element is the fact that their own account was used. So, they were defrauded quite independently of anything I did or didn’t do. So they are choosing basically to put the entire weight of the responsibility on just me.

In all three cases, the fraudsters transferred money into other Nedbank accounts and created new beneficiaries on our case studies’ profiles.

KALYANI PILLAY/SABRIC: When they are opening the same bank account in the same bank, it allows for easier and quicker transfer of the money.

In some cases, however, the beneficiary allegedly sells his or her account to the syndicates.

KALYANI PILLAY/SABRIC: They like to use that modus operandi because it hides them, because you find the runner, the person whose account it went through, because the banks in terms of complying with FICA, will be able to say this is who this person, this is where he lives.

DEVI: So, if somebody does that can you track them down?

ANTON DE WET: Absolutely, so what we would do is we work very closely with police, we work closely with SABRIC and the Hawks on instances where there’s fraud and we follow that up accordingly.

Dr Lues’s R735 000 was transferred to two newly created beneficiaries over two days.

DR. LUES: They actually took my maximum overdraft and the cash and the excess bond I had on my house that they all put into an account and threw it over into two of their accounts.

ADV CLIVE PILLAY: They maximise their pot. And then to confuse the bank, they then cipher it off into a number of smaller accounts.

DEVI: The shuffling process that happens before the money finally leaves your account, is what should raise alarm bells?

ADV CLIVE PILLAY: If that activity is completely at variance to your normal banking profile, one would then think that would raise a red flag.

Dr. Lues discovered and reported the fraud two days after it happened. The bank managed to retrieve R137 000 of the transferred money, not yet withdrawn.

DEVI LINK: The biggest chunk of the almost R600-thousand was used to buy foreign currency. The rest of the money was spent on things like air tickets, clothes, shoes and sunglasses.

Prof Kruger’s R85-thousand was also moved to a newly created beneficiary and withdrawn in the early hours of the morning.

DEVI LINK: Three thousand of the R85-thousand was withdrawn in cash at various ATM’s here at Montecasino. The rest of the money was withdrawn on the gambling floor and according to Nedbank the criminals usually buy chips, then pretend to play, before cashing in the money in.

The hours at which these transactions took place, are typical of these syndicates.

Danny: They go into your account, they look at when you receive your salary, how active are you in terms of going to your bank and looking at what your balance are etc so now they start planning, and when they are ready they log into your bank account normally over a weekend during evenings or late at night.

The bank detected the fraudulent transaction three hours after the withdrawal and prevented a further 25-thousand from being transferred.

FRANZ KRUGER: One would have expected them to give me a call to say: “Look there is something going on. Not only did they not contact me, but their own staff were not aware of what had happened.

Nedbank admits to the delay in communication, but says the system has since been improved.

ANTON DE WET: We’ve closed that loop out. We now have the call made directly from the fraud prevention unit. So, we hope and trust that we able to get to clients much quicker.

Noel’s R150-thousand was transferred to Fielding Tlali, but the bank didn’t detect the transfer and he lost it all.

DEVI LINK: Five thousand of Noel’s R150 000 was withdrawn in cash at this ATM in Turf Club Street, Turffontein. The other 145-thousand was used to buy foreign currency.

We called Fielding Tlali. He denied knowing anything about the R150-thousand transfer.

VOICE OF FIELDING TLALI: No, no, no, M’am, no such amount has reached me. I am not know that Gardner, I do not know no such thing.

PRODUCER: Do you have a Nedbank account?

VOICE OF FIELDING TLALI: I actually had one last year, but I have no longer one now.

Fielding Tlali’s account was closed by Nedbank after the incident.
After months without answers, Noel suddenly received an offer from the bank last week to refund all his money.

DEVI: It looks like its only been Carte Blanche that’s knocking on the door with this particular case that suddenly an offer was made.

ANTON: The money that was transferred fraudulently out of his account, went into an account where we had picked up fraudulent activity and our own internal system should have flagged that. Had we been a little bit quicker, we would have avoided the loss.

Professor Kruger, however, has only been offered half of the money he‘s lost.

DEVI: You can’t be half guilty though?

Anton: We felt that our response wasn’t as fast as it might have been and that we looked and offered, the settlement is on condition that we actually do scrub that PC.

The bank has yet to decide on a settlement for Dr. Lues, pending finalisation of their investigation.
Dr. Lues has opened a fraud case with the police and has taken Nedbank to the banking ombudsman.

ANTON DE WET: We’re talking around three people who have had awful incidences and they feel out of pocket. Against those three people where there have been losses incurred, we have nine thousand cases where we’ve saved any loss over the last five years.

FRANZ KRUGER: One of the things that this thing really brought home to me is how vulnerable one is online.

While banks are trying to stave off cyber crime attacks, techno savvy thieves are thinking up new schemes every day. So, be vigilant. Your bank has a responsibility to look after your money, but the buck ultimately stops with you.

ADV CLIVE PILLAY: They maximise their pot. And then to confuse the bank, they then cipher it off into a number of smaller accounts. DEVI: The shuffling process that happens before the money finally leaves your account, is what should raise alarm bells? ADV CLIVE PILLAY: If that activity is completely at variance to your normal banking profile, one would then think that would raise a red flag. Dr. Lues discovered and reported the fraud two days after it happened. The bank managed to retrieve R137 000 of the transferred money, not yet withdrawn. DEVI LINK: The biggest chunk of the almost R600-thousand was used to buy foreign currency. The rest of the money was spent on things like air tickets, clothes, shoes and sunglasses. Prof Kruger’s R85-thousand was also moved to a newly created beneficiary and withdrawn in the early hours of the morning. DEVI LINK: Three thousand of the R85-thousand was withdrawn in cash at various ATM’s here at Montecasino. The rest of the money was withdrawn on the gambling floor and according to Nedbank the criminals usually buy chips, then pretend to play, before cashing in the money in. The hours at which these transactions took place, are typical of these syndicates. Danny: They go into your account, they look at when you receive your salary, how active are you in terms of going to your bank and looking at what your balance are etc so now they start planning, and when they are ready they log into your bank account normally over a weekend during evenings or late at night. The bank detected the fraudulent transaction three hours after the withdrawal and prevented a further 25-thousand from being transferred. FRANZ KRUGER: One would have expected them to give me a call to say: “Look there is something going on. Not only did they not contact me, but their own staff were not aware of what had happened. Nedbank admits to the delay in communication, but says the system has since been improved. ANTON DE WET: We’ve closed that loop out. We now have the call made directly from the fraud prevention unit. So, we hope and trust that we able to get to clients much quicker. Noel’s R150-thousand was transferred to Fielding Tlali, but the bank didn’t detect the transfer and he lost it all. DEVI LINK: Five thousand of Noel’s R150 000 was withdrawn in cash at this ATM in Turf Club Street, Turffontein. The other 145-thousand was used to buy foreign currency. We called Fielding Tlali. He denied knowing anything about the R150-thousand transfer. VOICE OF FIELDING TLALI: No, no, no, M’am, no such amount has reached me. I am not know that Gardner, I do not know no such thing. PRODUCER: Do you have a Nedbank account? VOICE OF FIELDING TLALI: I actually had one last year, but I have no longer one now. Fielding Tlali’s account was closed by Nedbank after the incident. After months without answers, Noel suddenly received an offer from the bank last week to refund all his money. DEVI: It looks like its only been Carte Blanche that’s knocking on the door with this particular case that suddenly an offer was made. ANTON: The money that was transferred fraudulently out of his account, went into an account where we had picked up fraudulent activity and our own internal system should have flagged that. Had we been a little bit quicker, we would have avoided the loss. Professor Kruger, however, has only been offered half of the money he‘s lost. DEVI: You can’t be half guilty though? Anton: We felt that our response wasn’t as fast as it might have been and that we looked and offered, the settlement is on condition that we actually do scrub that PC. The bank has yet to decide on a settlement for Dr. Lues, pending finalisation of their investigation. Dr. Lues has opened a fraud case with the police and has taken Nedbank to the banking ombudsman. ANTON DE WET: We’re talking around three people who have had awful incidences and they feel out of pocket. Against those three people where there have been losses incurred, we have nine thousand cases where we’ve saved any loss over the last five years. FRANZ KRUGER: One of the things that this thing really brought home to me is how vulnerable one is online. While banks are trying to stave off cyber crime attacks, techno savvy thieves are thinking up new schemes every day. So, be vigilant. Your bank has a responsibility to look after your money, but the buck ultimately stops with you. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Unbeknown to you, a sim swop is done on your phone. The criminal then hacks into your banking details, transfers all your money to another account and leave you with nothing.
metadata.Summary: You might only think there is something wrong with your phone signal - your service provider is busy with maintenance in the area or it's just one more "bad signal day". Think again and be aware - because during this time that your phone is not working, an illegal and unauthorised sim swop could be taking place - directing all your messages to the criminal's phone, including your bank's One Time Pins (OTP's), with which you authorise transactions on your bank accounts.
metadata.Further information: How the criminal gains access to the victim's online banking details is still unclear. Most of our case studies say they know what phishing scams are and they haven't entered their details into any of these websites. All the case studies have been long-standing Nedbank clients. The scam works as follows: - without the victims knowledge or authorisation, a sim swop is done on his/her Vodacom phone - all mesages, including all One Time Pins to authorise online banking transactions, are then send to the criminal's phone who has done the sim swop - the criminal uses the victim's banking details to log into their online banking - the criminal then withdraws from the victim's credit, bond, overdraft etc to the maximum limit and transfers all this money into the victim's current account, before paying it into another Nedbank account - all of the transactions are authorised via OTP's which are sent to the criminal's cellphone instead of the victims, thanks to the sim swop - the money is withdrawn from the criminal's account (sometimes in cash) and becomes, according to Nedbank, untraceable It seems to be a quite sophisticated scam
